h1: Do markets see what the polls miss?
dek: Polls and prediction markets are both trying to tell us who becomes president of France in 2027. They don't always agree. This page shows where, and by how much.

h2a: Two readings of the same race
subA: Each row shows a candidate's chance according to ● polls, turned into a probability by simulation, and according to ◆ markets, read from Polymarket prices. The bar is the gap.

read1: The biggest disagreement is about Marine Le Pen. Polls put her far ahead in the first round and ahead in every runoff pairing tested, so a model built only on polls makes her a heavy favourite. Traders are much more cautious. They may be pricing in a late consolidation against her in the runoff, the fragility of polls this far out, or legal and political risks that polls cannot capture.
read2: Markets also keep a few names alive that polls barely register. David Lisnard polls under 3% yet trades as a real outsider, and Jordan Bardella keeps some value even though pollsters stopped testing him once Le Pen declared. Information, hedging or thin trading: that is exactly the kind of question this page is built to surface.
noteT: Handle the runoff view with care
note: The "who advances to the runoff" market is thin: about {{vq}} traded, against {{vw}} on the winner market. Its prices add up to roughly {{sum}} when two finalists should make 200%, so small candidates look more likely than they are.

subF: Choose a candidate: ● polls (chance of winning, derived from surveys by the simulation described in Method) and ◆ markets (chance of winning, weekly average of prices) are two probabilities of the same event, plotted on the same scale. The shaded area is the gap between the two lines. Hover or tap a numbered marker to read its note.
noteF: Each week, the simulation (medium uncertainty, same parameters as in Method) is run on the first-round and runoff polls of the previous 30 days. The poll line breaks when no survey was published in that period. Markets are weekly averages of daily prices. This chart does not depend on the comparison settings, whose chances rest on the last 60 days of polls.

m1: Polls to probabilities. Each simulation draws one recent first-round poll at random, adds polling error that grows with a candidate's score, and takes the top two. The runoff winner is then drawn from the average of head-to-head polls for that pair, plus error. Pairs never polled are decided by relative first-round strength. 20,000 simulations per view. Poll-based chances assume the candidate is on the ballot.
m2: Uncertainty. Seven months out, French polls can miss badly: five months before the 2022 vote, Jean-Luc Mélenchon was underestimated by more than ten points. "Medium" adds roughly 1.5 points plus 20% of a candidate's score to first-round error, and 6 points to runoff error. Change the setting to see how sensitive the poll view is.
m3: Markets. Implied probabilities from the last traded price on two Polymarket markets: the overall winner, and who advances to the second round. Prices are shown as data only. Polymarket is not authorised in France; this page does not link to it or encourage trading.
m4: Sources. Polls compiled by the open MieuxVoter/presidentielle2027 repository (MIT licence), from polls published under the supervision of the Commission des sondages. Each poll remains the property of its institute and sponsor.
aboutP1: L'Écart is an academic research project, designed and built by Luke Segault. For the 2027 French presidential election, it compares the chances of winning read from prediction-market prices with those that can be derived from polls, to see where they diverge and why.
aboutOnly: For academic research only. This site is not a forecast, is not advice, and is not an invitation to bet.
